title: Thimble and Pippin's Tart Surprise
markdown:
The little girl’s breathing deepened, a soft rhythmic sigh that told Thimble and Pippin their window of opportunity was wide open. From their cozy spot on the worn patchwork rug they watched her slumber, a warm safe island in the quiet darkness. Thimble, a fluffy white bunny whose ears seemed almost too long for his head, nudged Pippin with his damp nose.

“Think she’s truly asleep, Pip?” A soft rustle like dry leaves.

Pippin, a sleek grey rat with bright intelligent eyes that missed nothing, whiskers twitching, nodded. “Deeply. The sandman has surely filled her eyelids with lead. And that means…”

“The bluebell woods.” Thimble’s ears shot up, quivering. He’d heard whispers on the night breeze about a secret midnight baking contest. Prizes legendary. Moonberry tarts simply divine. Pippin, ever the strategist, loved a good challenge. Thimble loved anything that promised a sweet taste of adventure.

A familiar flutter in Thimble’s chest. What if he got distracted by a particularly shiny beetle again? What if he missed the whole point because he was staring at a funny-shaped cloud? His usually soft paws felt cold and strangely heavy.

“The prize,” Pippin murmured, barely disturbing the quiet, “is said to be a lifetime supply of dandelion puffs. And more importantly, bragging rights. Imagine it, Thimble. The best bakers in the woods.” He looked toward the darkened window, garden fence a dark line against starlit sky. “If we don’t go, we’ll never know if we could have won. And the woods will be buzzing with tales of winners by sunrise, and we’ll have nothing to contribute but silence.”

That silence, being left out of the gossip, was a powerful motivator.

With a shared determined glance they were off. Silent scramble down the hallway, daring squeeze through a gap in the kitchen door, cool damp grass of the garden. A nimble dash across the lawn, squeeze under the sturdy fence, and they were in the hushed mysterious bluebell woods. Cool air: damp earth, decaying leaves, faint sweet perfume of countless bluebells. A deep hush, not complete silence. Some parts draped in delicate shimmering bunting between ancient oaks; others shrouded in theatrical expectant darkness.

“Bunting,” Thimble whispered, eyes wide, reflecting faint starlight. “Look, Pip. Like a party waiting to happen.” He hopped toward a particularly colourful string of paper flags, vibrant patterns almost pulling him from the mission.

Pippin grabbed his ear gently, firm but kind. “Focus, Thimble. Bunting means some of them want to be seen. But the contest is meant to be secret. The truly brilliant bakers operate in the shadows, not under bright flags. That means stealthy, not starstruck.”

They tiptoed past squirrels, bushy tails twitching, meticulously arranging tiny acorn cupcakes on mossy platters. Hushed arguments about frosting consistency—was a swirl too much?—a low intriguing hum. Further on, a badger emerging from his sett scowled and hissed, “Silence. This is a clandestine culinary competition. No chatter, only tasting.”

A firefly, tiny light blinking erratically like a miniature disco ball, zipped past Thimble’s nose.

“Ooh, a dancing star.” Captivated, he bounded after it. The firefly, perhaps amused, led him deeper, light a tantalizing beacon, pulling him from Pippin’s urgent calls. He stumbled, paws sinking into soft yielding moss. Blinked. Firefly gone. Trees loomed taller, darker. A shiver, not of cold. Familiar paralysis. Fluffy white tail tucked so tight it was practically glued to his belly. The full panic of losing his way, focus evaporated.

Just as he was about to let out a small frightened squeak, Pippin’s urgent whisper, laced with discovery.

“Thimble. Over here. I think I found it.”

He scrambled back, heart thudding, and found Pippin peering into a hidden clearing. Under the moon: tables laden with exquisite gravity-defying baked goods. Mushroom meringues. Dewdrop financiers that sparkled like tiny gems. And yes, the legendary moonberry tarts, glistening like dark jewels. A gentle murmur of admiration from the judges: a wise old owl with spectacles, a stern-faced hedgehog whose prickles seemed to vibrate with critical evaluation. They had found the contest. The first entries were already being presented.

Pippin’s whiskers drooped. “We’re too late to bake for the main judging, Thimble. We’ve missed the deadline.”

Thimble’s ears drooped too. Then his eyes fell on a small empty space at the very end of a long table, clearly meant for latecomers.

“We can still bake something, Pip. We just need to be quick. Really quick.”

Pippin’s eyes lit up. “You’re right. I’ve got the flour and sugar in my satchel. Let’s find some berries, fast.” Thimble, eager to prove he could be focused when it mattered, spotted a bush laden with dark plump berries, glistening enticingly. He filled his paws, barely noticing their slightly duller sheen, or that they seemed smaller than the illustrations he’d seen.

They set to work with frantic energy, paws a blur. Pippin mixed dry ingredients with practiced speed. Thimble mashed berries with all his might. As he tipped the mash into the batter, he noticed the sharp decidedly sour scent. Not sweet juicy moonberries. Common elderberries, still a little unripe, rather tart. A tremor. His fault. Completely. The half-baked dough felt wrong and claggy. The vinegary smell stung. Nearby leaves seemed to mock him.

He looked at Pippin, already dusted with flour, brow furrowed. Thimble swallowed, loud in his own ears.

“Pip,” he whispered, trembling, “I grabbed the wrong berries. These are… they’re sour.”

Pippin stopped, nimble paws still, a cloud of flour hanging. He looked at the batter, then at Thimble’s crestfallen face. A flicker of disappointment. Then a sigh, a small puff of flour.

“It’s all right, Thimble. We can’t change it now. Let’s just bake them and hope for the best.”

They presented a small slightly lopsided tart. Not as plump or lusciously sweet as the other entries. Flavour a surprise: a tangy almost electric kick that made the hedgehog judge wrinkle his nose most dramatically. Thimble, gathering courage, stepped forward and explained.

“We’re very sorry,” he mumbled, ears drooping, “but we wanted to enter, and I, uh, got a bit mixed up with the berries.”

A hush. Then an old dormouse, who had baked the most delicate acorn cookies Thimble had ever seen, spoke up.

“Well, that certainly is distinctive. But the effort is commendable. And the story of your haste is quite charming.”

A wise old robin, nearby branch: “And admitting your mistake so quickly? That shows a great deal of character, young bunny.”

The owl judge hooted softly, adjusting spectacles. “Indeed. While your berries may be unconventional, your honesty and teamwork are not. Your tart, though tart indeed, has spirit. And spirit is something we value highly in the woods.” To their utter astonishment they were awarded a special Spirit of the Woods ribbon, moss and silver thread.

Hopping home, first hint of dawn pink and gold, Thimble felt a lightness he hadn’t known. He had made a silly daft mistake. Admitting it had not led to disaster. He looked at Pippin, already planning their next culinary adventure, bright eyes sparkling.

“That was quite a race, wasn’t it?” Pippin nudged him gently.

Thimble smiled, genuine, unfettered. They slipped back under the garden fence. The bluebell woods were beginning to stir. Thimble noticed a single bluebell, petals a vibrant deep sapphire, swaying. He paused, admiring its quiet beauty, without the usual overwhelming urge to hop away and chase a fleeting thought. He simply appreciated it. The ribbon, slightly sticky with elderberry, travelled home in Pippin’s satchel, and the little girl’s breathing, still deep, did not notice two bakers returning to the rug.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing night-time woodland adventure for older children
